concept.name: Anchoring bias
concept.definition: The tendency for judgments and estimates to be biased toward an initially encountered reference value (the anchor), even when it is arbitrary or irrelevant, introduced as a heuristic by Tversky and Kahneman (1974). Adjustments away from the anchor are typically insufficient, so final estimates cluster near it.
concept.intuition: The first number you hear - a purchase price, a 52-week high, an analyst target - quietly drags every later estimate toward itself.
concept.mechanics: In the classic experiment, a rigged wheel stopping at 10 versus 65 moved estimates of African UN membership from 25% to 45%. Explained by anchoring-and-insufficient-adjustment and by selective accessibility of anchor-consistent information; in markets, purchase prices, round numbers, and historical highs and lows act as anchors.
concept.failure_modes: Extremely transparent or implausible anchors sometimes fail to replicate the effect, and self-generated anchors behave differently from provided ones. The bias is notably resistant to debiasing: explicit warnings and monetary incentives mostly fail to remove it.
concept.misconceptions: Anchors need not be plausible or consciously accepted to work, and experts (for example real-estate agents given listing prices) are affected while denying it. Using a genuinely informative reference price is not anchoring bias.
concept.example: A trader anchors on the $150 price at which she bought a stock and reads $120 as 'cheap' relative to it, instead of evaluating the business at its current price.
